The first thing the city forgot was the name of a small street behind the railway station. Its sign remained, blue enamel under pigeon dust, but the letters had become meaningless. Delivery drivers pointed at it. Residents opened their mouths and frowned. Eventually, someone taped a handwritten notice beneath it: YOU KNOW THE ONE.

For a while, that was enough.

Cities survive on arrangements less official than names. There is the bakery beside the place that used to sell lamps. There is the corner where the wind steals umbrellas. There is the apartment with the yellow curtains, though the curtains have been green for years. People found the little street by remembering what they had done there: bought flowers, lost a glove, kissed someone unsuitable.

Then the river forgot which way to flow.

It did not reverse. That would have been dramatic, and the city disliked drama before lunch. Instead, the river hesitated. Water gathered in thoughtful folds. Leaves circled beneath the bridges. A fisherman lowered his hook and watched the float remain perfectly still, as though the world had become a painting whose artist had stepped away.

At city hall, a committee was formed. The committee commissioned a report. The report described an unprecedented navigational uncertainty within the municipal watercourse and recommended further observation. By then, three clocks had forgotten eleven, a tram had forgotten its final stop, and every statue in the central square had turned slightly toward home.

Mara noticed none of this immediately. She repaired books in a basement beneath the public library, where the weather arrived only as dampness in the walls. Her work involved small, defensible victories. A loose page could be secured. A broken spine could be reinforced. Even a book dropped in a bathtub might recover, provided nobody tried to hurry it.

One morning, she opened an atlas and found a blank space where the city should have been.

The surrounding countryside remained: hills shaded brown, reservoirs pale blue, roads threading between villages. But the city was gone. In its place lay an oval of clean paper. Mara touched it with one finger. The paper felt warm.

Upstairs, the librarians were arguing over the word for staircase.

“The steps,” one said.

“Yes, but the whole thing.”

“The climbing arrangement.”

“That cannot possibly be right.”

Mara took her coat.

Outside, the city seemed embarrassed. Shopkeepers stood beneath signs they could no longer read. A bus announced its destination as Somewhere Beyond the Hospital. In the square, pigeons landed cautiously, uncertain whether pigeons had always been permitted.

She went to the oldest person she knew, a retired locksmith named Ivo who lived above a shuttered cinema. He listened without interruption while she described the atlas. Then he made tea in two mismatched cups.

“It happened once before,” he said.

“When?”

“I don’t remember.”

“That seems inconvenient.”

“It was inconvenient then, too.”

He brought out a tin box containing a tram ticket, a brass button, a photograph of an empty chair, and a folded sheet of paper. On the paper, in handwriting almost worn away, someone had written: Begin with what happened here.

“Who wrote that?” Mara asked.

Ivo studied the page.

“I believe,” he said, “someone who wanted us to manage without them.”

That afternoon, Mara carried a table from the library into the square. She placed a notebook on it and made a sign: TELL ME SOMETHING YOU REMEMBER.

At first, people offered facts.

The station opened in 1894.

The northern bridge was forty metres long.

The mayor had served three terms.

Mara wrote everything down. Nothing changed.

Then a woman carrying groceries stopped beside the table.

“My father used to wait right there,” she said, pointing toward the fountain. “When my mother finished work, he pretended he had only just arrived. Sometimes he waited an hour.”

The fountain shivered. Water rose from its dry mouth.

After that, a queue formed.

A butcher remembered being frightened of his first customer. A schoolteacher remembered stealing cherries from a garden now occupied by a bank. Two brothers disagreed about the color of a dog they had loved. Mara recorded both colors. Behind her, the statues slowly turned back.

Nobody remembered anything important on purpose. They remembered soup, arguments, summer heat, the smell of a particular stairwell. They remembered the shame of an unkind remark. They remembered being forgiven without having to ask. As Mara listened, the square grew loud with people interrupting one another, correcting dates, and calling neighbors over to help.

By evening, the river was moving again.

But the blank space in the atlas remained.

Mara sat beneath a streetlamp, exhausted. Her notebook was full. Around her, people had begun telling stories without waiting for their turn.

Ivo arrived carrying bread.

“Perhaps there is something you haven’t asked,” he said.

“What?”

He tore the loaf in half.

“What do you remember?”

She almost said she had been too busy. Instead, she remembered arriving at nineteen with a suitcase whose handle broke outside the station. She had stood in the rain, angry enough to cry. A stranger carrying a sleeping child stopped and offered her a length of red cord from his pocket. Together, awkwardly, they tied the suitcase shut. She never learned his name.

As she spoke, the streetlamp brightened.

In the library basement, ink spread across the atlas, restoring houses, bridges, and the bend of the river.

Mara returned the next morning and found one thing missing: the little street behind the station. She asked among the residents, but none could recall its former name.

The council eventually proposed Railway Approach. Before the new sign could be ordered, however, a resident submitted another suggestion. It passed by a narrow vote.

Years later, visitors occasionally asked why such an ordinary street was called Red Cord.

There was usually someone nearby willing to tell them.
